objectives: Trace the origin of formal veterinary education from Bourgelat to modern schools.
Connect veterinary medicine to professional institutions (AVMA, WSAVA, WOAH).
Explain the One Health framework + Schwabe's foundational synthesis.

slides.title: Origins: Bourgelat, the École Vétérinaire of Lyon, and the birth of a profession
slides.body:
Veterinary medicine as a formal discipline was born in **Lyon, France, in 1761**, when **Claude Bourgelat** founded the world's first veterinary school — the **École Nationale Vétérinaire de Lyon** — with backing from Louis XV. Bourgelat (1712-1779), a riding-academy director + jurist, had been frustrated by the catastrophic European rinderpest (cattle plague) epizootics of the 17th-18th centuries that destroyed millions of cattle + the empirical, often-disastrous farriery + cow-leech tradition of the day. He argued that animal disease could be studied scientifically, taught systematically, + practised professionally — exactly the Enlightenment logic Boerhaave + the Edinburgh school had applied to human medicine.

**Why Lyon, why 1761**:
- Rinderpest swept Europe repeatedly (1709-1714, 1742-1760), killing ~200 million cattle by some estimates + devastating rural economies. Governments wanted trained personnel.
- Bourgelat was a friend of Diderot + d'Alembert + contributed equine articles to the *Encyclopédie* — Enlightenment networks supported the project.
- A second school followed in **Alfort (Maisons-Alfort, near Paris) in 1765**, also under Bourgelat.
- Within decades: Vienna (1765, Ludwig Scotti), Turin (1769), Copenhagen (1773), Hannover (1778), London Veterinary College (1791, Charles Vial de Sainbel), Edinburgh Dick Vet (1823, William Dick).

**Comparative medicine from the start**: Bourgelat explicitly taught that animal + human anatomy + pathology shared common principles — a position that anticipated Schwabe's *Veterinary Medicine and Human Health* (1984) by two centuries. He insisted students dissect across species + study horses, cattle, dogs, + comparative human cadavers.

**United States — early professionalization**:
- 1854: New York College of Veterinary Surgeons (private).
- 1879: **Iowa State** opens the first land-grant veterinary college — model for state veterinary schools through the **Morrill Land-Grant Acts (1862, 1890)**. By 1900 ~10 US schools; today 33 AVMA-accredited US schools + 19 internationally.
- 1863: **American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA)** founded in New York City as the United States Veterinary Medical Association — sets accreditation, ethics, scope of practice, advocacy, + the practice act framework adopted by every US state.

**Britain**:
- Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (**RCVS**) founded 1844 by Royal Charter — credentialing + regulation.
- The London + Edinburgh schools fed empire-wide veterinary services administering rinderpest control, glanders eradication in horses, anthrax research (under Pasteur + Greenfield + Koch).

**Founding intellectual moves**: by 1900, veterinary medicine had its own anatomy, pathology, infectious disease, surgery, pharmacology, + public-health curricula — separate from but parallel to human medicine. The split has narrowed since the One Health revival of the 2000s.

slides.title: James Herriot, the cultural face of veterinary practice, and the 20th-century profession
slides.body:
**James Herriot** — the pen name of **James Alfred Wight (1916-1995)** — published *If Only They Could Talk* (1970) and *All Creatures Great and Small* (1972), semi-autobiographical accounts of a Yorkshire mixed-practice vet in the 1930s-1950s. The books + BBC TV adaptations (1978-1990, 2020+) became the dominant global image of the country veterinarian: gentle, observant, comfortable with both farm + companion animals, embedded in rural community. Herriot's narratives — calving cows in winter, treating Pekingese-of-wealthy-widow, Tricki Woo, mentoring young assistants under the irascible Siegfried Farnon — humanized + romanticized the profession + arguably drove decades of veterinary-school applications.

**What Herriot's era captured (and didn't)**:
- **Captured**: mixed practice (large + small animal in one practitioner); pre-antibiotic + early-antibiotic era (sulfonamides 1930s, penicillin from 1944, broad-spectrum antibiotics 1950s); arrival of magnesium-deficiency recognition in cattle; transition from horse-as-prime-mover to tractor; cesarean section in cattle becoming routine.
- **Didn't capture**: the technological + corporate transformation that followed.

**Mid-20th-century professional change**:
- **Decline of equine + draft-animal practice** as mechanization replaced horses (US horse population fell from ~25 M in 1915 to ~5 M by 1960 — though it has recovered to ~7-10 M as pleasure + sport).
- **Rise of companion-animal practice**: post-WWII pet keeping exploded; the small-animal practice now ~70-80% of US veterinary economy. Banfield + VCA + Mars Petcare consolidated thousands of practices since the 1990s.
- **Production-animal industrial scale**: dairy + beef + poultry + swine moved from family farms to integrated, large-scale operations needing food-animal vets, herd-health consultants, + state veterinarians for regulatory work.
- **Women in veterinary medicine**: from <5% of US graduates in 1965 to >85% by 2020 — the most rapidly feminized of the major health professions.

**The World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA)**: founded **1959 (London)**, federates national companion-animal associations from ~80+ countries; issues global guidelines for vaccination, nutrition, pain management, dental care, hereditary disease, + the WSAVA Body Condition Score chart used worldwide.

**Specialization arrived late but fast**: the **American Board of Veterinary Specialties (ABVS)** now recognizes 22 specialty colleges (surgery, internal medicine, oncology, cardiology, dermatology, ophthalmology, neurology, anesthesiology, dentistry, behavior, lab animal, pathology, microbiology, radiology, theriogenology, emergency + critical care, sports medicine, zoo, preventive medicine, nutrition, toxicology, pharmacology). The European College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (ECVIM-CA) + parallel European boards mirror the US system. Specialty referral centers + teaching hospitals now perform CT, MRI, advanced surgery, interventional radiology, chemotherapy, + radiation oncology routinely on companion animals.

slides.title: WOAH, AVMA, WSAVA, + the One Health synthesis (Schwabe → 2020s)
slides.body:
**WOAH — World Organisation for Animal Health** (founded 1924, Paris, as the **Office International des Épizooties / OIE**; rebranded to **WOAH** in 2022): the global intergovernmental authority for animal-health standards + disease reporting. 183 member countries. Manages:
- **WOAH Terrestrial + Aquatic Animal Health Codes**: legally referenced standards for international animal-trade biosecurity.
- **WAHIS (World Animal Health Information System)**: real-time global disease reporting (FMD, HPAI, ASF, lumpy-skin disease, PPR, etc.).
- **Reference laboratories + collaborating centres**: ~300 worldwide.
- **The Tripartite** (with **WHO + FAO**, joined by UNEP in 2022 to form the **Quadripartite**) sets the global One Health agenda — antimicrobial resistance, zoonoses, food safety, environmental health.

**AVMA today**: ~105,000 US members; sets practice standards (Principles of Veterinary Medical Ethics); accredits all 33 US + 18 international schools through the **Council on Education (COE)**; publishes the *JAVMA* + *AJVR*; runs the AVMA Group Health + Life Insurance + Trust; advocates for the profession in Washington, DC. The **American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA)** parallels AVMA with practice-accreditation focus.

**One Health — the integrative paradigm**:
- **Calvin Schwabe** (UC Davis epidemiologist, 1927-2006), in *Veterinary Medicine and Human Health* (1st ed. 1964; 3rd ed. **1984**), coined the term **'one medicine'** + argued explicitly that human + animal + environmental health are inseparable. Schwabe trained in parasitology in Lebanon + studied hydatid disease (Echinococcus) — a textbook zoonosis transmitted dog↔sheep↔human.
- The modern formulation **'One Health'** spread in the 2000s — Wildlife Conservation Society's **Manhattan Principles** (2004, William Karesh + colleagues), the One Health Initiative (Roger Mahr, Laura Kahn, Bruce Kaplan, Tom Monath, Lonnie King), + adoption by WHO + FAO + WOAH.
- Drivers: SARS (2002-03), H5N1 (2003+), monkeypox emergence, Nipah, Ebola spillover, antimicrobial resistance, MERS (2012), Ebola West Africa (2014), Zika (2015), **COVID-19 (2019+)**, **H5N1 dairy-cattle outbreak (2024)**. Roughly 75% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic.

**Schwabe's three pillars** of One Medicine (paraphrased):
1. **Comparative medicine**: human + animal disease share mechanisms + treatments.
2. **Zoonotic disease control**: cannot be done in either domain alone.
3. **Food safety + nutrition**: animals are both the route of human nutrition + the route of foodborne illness.

**Practical consequences today**:
- **Antimicrobial stewardship**: ~70% of medically important antibiotics in the US (by weight) are used in food animals. WOAH + WHO + FAO joint AMR strategy.
- **Pandemic preparedness**: surveillance at the wildlife-livestock-human interface (PREDICT, USAID; EcoHealth Alliance under **Peter Daszak**; WCS under **William Karesh** + others).
- **Food security**: livestock provide ~17% of global calories, ~33% of protein; climate change + drought + zoonoses threaten supply.
- **Companion-animal welfare**: increasingly central to public-health framing — bond, attachment, mental-health benefits of pets, plus shared-environment exposure (Lyme, leishmania, leptospirosis).

**Modern veterinary medicine** sits at the intersection of clinical practice (small animal + large animal + exotic), industrial-scale agriculture, wildlife conservation, public health, biomedical research, + emerging-disease surveillance. The discipline that began with Bourgelat treating colicked horses + plagued cattle now coordinates global pandemic response — a trajectory Schwabe predicted exactly.

question.question: Trace how a 1761 founding event led to a 21st-century pandemic-response framework
question.goal: Connect Bourgelat's 1761 founding of the Lyon school to the Quadripartite (WOAH + WHO + FAO + UNEP) One Health structure of today, identifying the intermediate institutions + intellectual moves.

Bourgelat's 1761 school of scientific animal medicine + Schwabe's 1964 'one medicine' synthesis + the 2004 Manhattan Principles + the 2022 Quadripartite together form a coherent ~260-year arc.

question.question: Why is Bourgelat's 1761 founding of the Lyon school treated as the birth of modern veterinary medicine?
options: Claude Bourgelat (1712-1779) founded the École Nationale Vétérinaire de Lyon in 1761 with royal backing — the **first formal, scientific, university-style veterinary school in the world**. It systematized animal medicine as a profession (rather than an empirical farriery + cow-leech trade), trained the first generation of credentialed veterinarians who staffed Alfort (1765), Vienna (1765), Turin (1769), London (1791), Edinburgh (1823), Iowa State (1879) + the rest of the global network, + embedded comparative medicine into the curriculum — anticipating Schwabe's 'one medicine' synthesis by two centuries. Without Bourgelat there is no AVMA (1863), no WSAVA, no WOAH/OIE (1924), no One Health framework. The model spread across Europe within decades + then globally — the Lyon school is the institutional ancestor of every modern veterinary school + every veterinary regulatory body.
question.explanation: Bourgelat's Lyon school (1761) was the first formal, scientific veterinary school + the institutional ancestor of every modern veterinary education + regulatory body. It also embedded comparative medicine from the start, anticipating Schwabe's One Health synthesis.

slides.workedSolution: Bourgelat founded the École Nationale Vétérinaire de Lyon in 1761 — the first scientific veterinary school. It professionalized animal medicine, trained the first credentialed veterinarians, spread to Alfort (1765), Vienna, Turin, London, Edinburgh, Iowa State, + embedded comparative medicine from the start. Without Lyon there is no AVMA, WSAVA, WOAH, or One Health framework.

question.question: A 2024 H5N1 outbreak appears in US dairy cattle, with sporadic mild human infections in dairy workers. Apply the Schwabe/One Health framework to organize a response.
question.scenario: Use Quadripartite + AVMA + USDA structures to mount a coordinated response.
question.modelAnswer: Apply One Health (Schwabe 1984; Manhattan Principles 2004) explicitly: (1) **Animal health pillar (WOAH/USDA APHIS)** — mandatory reporting of HPAI-positive dairy herds under federal order; movement controls + biosecurity at the farm level; trace-back + trace-forward; PCR + serology surveillance; coordination with WOAH WAHIS reporting. (2) **Human health pillar (CDC/WHO)** — surveillance of dairy + poultry workers via active case finding, baseline serology, PPE distribution, antiviral prophylaxis (oseltamivir) for exposed; monitor for any human-to-human transmission signal. (3) **Food safety (FDA/FAO)** — confirm pasteurization inactivates virus (it does); surveillance of bulk-tank milk; risk communication to public on raw-milk dangers. (4) **Environmental + wildlife (UNEP/USFWS)** — wild-bird surveillance (waterfowl flyways), mammal spillover monitoring (foxes, seals, sea lions, marine mammals). (5) **Antimicrobial + biosecurity policy** — secondary-bacterial-pneumonia preparedness. (6) **Communication** — the AVMA + WSAVA + state veterinarians coordinate guidance to practising vets, who often are the first to recognize unusual signs in cattle. (7) **Research** — characterize the bovine PB2 mutations + receptor-binding profile; develop bovine + human vaccine candidates (Boehringer Ingelheim, CSL Seqirus). (8) **Long-term**: integrate findings into the next pandemic-preparedness cycle. The Schwabe framework explicitly insists that none of these pillars can succeed alone — a poultry-only or human-only response misses the bovine reservoir + a livestock-only response misses spillover. Daszak/EcoHealth Alliance + Karesh/WCS-era wildlife-livestock-human surveillance is precisely the architecture needed.
question.rubric: Identifies the One Health framework (Schwabe; Manhattan Principles), invokes the Quadripartite (WOAH + WHO + FAO + UNEP) by function, coordinates animal + human + environment + food pillars, names institutional roles (USDA APHIS, CDC, FDA, AVMA), + recognises that integrated response is the defining feature of the framework.

question.question: Approximately how many years separate Bourgelat's founding of the Lyon school from the founding of the AVMA? How many years from the AVMA founding to the OIE (now WOAH)?
acceptedAnswers: ~102 years (Bourgelat to AVMA); ~61 years (AVMA to OIE/WOAH)
question.explanation: Bourgelat founded Lyon in **1761**. AVMA was founded in **1863**, so 1863 − 1761 = **102 years** later. The OIE (now WOAH) was founded in **1924**, so 1924 − 1863 = **61 years** after AVMA. This timeline traces the institutionalization arc: national school (1761) → national professional association (1863) → international intergovernmental authority (1924) → Tripartite (early 2000s) → Quadripartite (2022). The accelerating cadence mirrors the globalization of animal disease + trade.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how James Herriot's portrayal of veterinary practice both captured + obscured the 20th-century transformation of the profession.
question.rubric: Mentions: (1) Herriot/James Alfred Wight's *All Creatures Great and Small* (1972) + BBC adaptations created the dominant cultural image of the country vet — mixed practice, rural community, gentle observation; humanized + romanticized the profession + drove generations of applicants. (2) Captured: the transition from horse to tractor, pre-antibiotic → antibiotic era, calving + farriery + everyday rural practice. (3) Obscured: the post-1970 transformation — collapse of mixed practice, rise of corporate small-animal chains (Banfield, VCA, Mars Petcare), industrial production agriculture, women becoming >85% of US graduates, specialty referral medicine with CT/MRI/oncology, and the rise of One Health/global zoonosis surveillance. (4) Concludes that Herriot's Yorkshire is a poignant snapshot of one moment in a profession that has industrialized, feminized, specialized, + globalized in ways his novels did not foresee.
